entities.name: Spurius Carvilius Maximus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Spurius Carvilius C. f. C. n., later surnamed Maximus, emerged as a pivotal military and political figure in the Roman Republic during the crucial decades of the Third Samnite War and the Pyrrhic War. As the first member of the plebeian gens Carvilia to achieve the consulship, which he held in 293 BCE and again in 272 BCE, Carvilius Maximus played a significant role in consolidating Roman dominance across central and southern Italy, embodying the rising power of the plebeian aristocracy within the evolving Roman state.

His first consulship in 293 BCE, alongside Lucius Papirius Cursor, saw him lead Roman legions to decisive victories against the Samnites. He besieged and captured Amiternum, Cominium, and Palumbinum, securing crucial strategic positions. Notably, during this campaign, he defeated a Samnite army near Aquilonia, recovering the bronze shields that the Samnites had used in a religious ceremony to inspire their troops, and distributing them as firewood to his soldiers. These triumphs earned him a splendid ovation and a formal triumph in Rome, during which he dedicated a temple to Fors Fortuna, funded by the spoils of war, and adorned the Capitoline with Samnite armor. His second consulship in 272 BCE, again with Papirius Cursor, was marked by the final stages of the Pyrrhic War and the subsequent subjugation of Tarentum and the Lucanians and Bruttians, marking the definitive establishment of Roman hegemony over Magna Graecia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Spurius Carvilius Maximus was a key figure in Rome's definitive subjugation of the Samnites and the consolidation of control over Magna Graecia, directly contributing to the formation of a unified Roman Italy. His career exemplifies the growing power of plebeian families and the military effectiveness that enabled Rome's expansion.
